name: Delhi–Chennai Highway

timeline.event: Four-laning of the Delhi–Mumbai and Mumbai–Chennai corridors begins under the Golden Quadrilateral project
The Delhi–Gurugram Expressway, a signal-free six- to eight-lane stretch out of Delhi, is completed
The old NH 8 and NH 4 are merged and renumbered as NH 48
Golden Quadrilateral programme declared substantially complete

history: NH 48 links Delhi and Chennai the long way round, sweeping down India's west coast and across the south through Jaipur, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Pune and Bengaluru. It was created in the 2010 renumbering by joining two of India's most famous roads: the old NH 8 from Delhi to Mumbai and the old NH 4 from Mumbai to Chennai. Together these form the western and southern sides of the Golden Quadrilateral, the four-sided network that connects India's four biggest metro cities. Both halves were among the very first stretches to be widened to four lanes when the Golden Quadrilateral began in 2001, and much of the route has since been taken to six lanes. The road begins in Delhi at Dhaula Kuan and finishes where it meets NH 16 on the edge of Chennai. Almost every big industrial belt in western and southern India — Gurugram, Bhiwadi, Vapi, Silvassa, Pune, Hosur, Sriperumbudur — grew up along it.
facts: About 2,807 km long, passing through seven states and union territories.
Carries two full sides of the Golden Quadrilateral: Delhi–Mumbai and Mumbai–Chennai.
Connects four of India's largest cities — Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Chennai — plus Jaipur, Ahmedabad, Surat and Pune.
The Delhi–Gurugram stretch is one of the busiest roads in India.
Between Mumbai and Pune it is paralleled by the Mumbai–Pune Expressway, India's first six-lane concrete expressway.
Inside Mumbai the highway runs as the Western Express Highway from Dahisar down to Bandra.
It starts at Dhaula Kuan in Delhi and ends where it joins NH 16 near Chennai.
The Kherki Daula toll plaza in Gurugram is one of the most-used toll plazas in the country.
significance: NH 48 is the money road of the Indian highway network. It strings together Delhi, Jaipur, Ahmedabad, Surat, Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru and Chennai — the ports, factories and IT hubs that produce a huge share of India's exports — so it carries more container and truck traffic than almost any other route. It is also a daily commuter road for millions: for people going into Gurugram, into Mumbai from Thane, into Pune, and into Chennai from Sriperumbudur.

travelNotes: Nobody drives the whole thing in one go — think of it as several famous road trips joined end to end. Delhi to Jaipur is about five hours, Mumbai to Pune about three on the parallel expressway, and Bengaluru to Chennai six to seven. The Delhi–Gurugram section jams badly on weekday mornings and evenings, the Vapi–Mumbai stretch is slow because of heavy container traffic, and December–January fog can crawl the Delhi–Jaipur leg. Dhaba culture is strong on the Rajasthan and Gujarat sections, and the Karnataka–Tamil Nadu section has good, modern highway food courts. October to March is the pleasantest season overall.
futureUpgrades: The Delhi–Mumbai Expressway is being built as a faster parallel route and will take a large share of long-distance traffic off the Delhi–Jaipur–Ahmedabad–Mumbai stretch.
The Bengaluru–Chennai Expressway (NE 7) will do the same for the Bengaluru–Chennai leg.
